answerlines: Babylon [or the Hanging Gardens of Babylon; or Bab-ilu; or Bab-ilim; or Bavel; or Babel; or Atlal Babil]

clues.text: During periods of waning power of empires centered on this city, it was ruled by Kassites.
One king from this city built the gate of Ishtar and ordered the destruction of the temple of Jerusalem.
According to Herodotus, this city had hundreds of gates, massive walls, and tribes that only consumed fish.
Sennacherib was murdered by his own sons in 689 BCE because of his destruction of this city.
Though it’s not Judea, this state was conquered by the Assyrian Sennacherib.
Although archaeologists haven’t found evidence of it, a terraced building in this city was legendarily built on the orders of Nebuchadnezzar II, whose wife was homesick for greenery.
The only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World which may not have actually existed were this city's Hanging Gardens.
A law code originating the phrase “an eye for an eye” was inscribed on a stele by this city’s king Hammurabi.
Name this Mesopotamian city-state, ruled by kings such as Nebuchadnezzar and Hammurabi, which was known for its hanging gardens.
Name this ancient Mesopotamian city in which a set of “hanging gardens” might have been built.
Artwork from this city includes the ruined Etemenanki (“eht-MEN-en-kee”) Temple.
This city lost control of the Median Wall after it was defeated at the Battle of Opis.
The “Cyrus cylinder” documents Cyrus’ conquest of this city and its last king Nabonidus.
A structure from this city depicting gold mušḫuššu dragons was reconstructed in the Pergamon Museum.
Rubble from this city was thrown into the Arakhtu Canal after its destruction by Sennacherib.
A basalt stele from this city depicts a ruler receiving divine inspiration from the sun god, Shamash.
The Etemenanki Ziggurat was built in this city, whose Ishtar Gate was the entrance to another building in it.
A no-longer-extant ziggurat in this city was dedicated to its patron deity, Marduk.
Marduk was the patron god of this city, whose king Nebuchadnezzar (“NEH-boo-cud-NEZ-er”) II may have built one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
Name this city in modern-day Iraq that was once home to the Hanging Gardens.

answerlines: Babylon [or the Babylonian Empire or the Neo-Babylonian Empire; accept Babel or Babylonia or Bābilim or Neo-Babylon; accept the Babylonian captivity]

clues.text: This capital’s social system divided status between awilum (“uh-WILL-um”), mushkenum (“mush-KEN-num”) and slave-like war∙dum.
Robert Koldewey excavated a structure in this city that contained reliefs of lions, aurochs, and dragon-like mušḫuššu.
This city’s Etemenanki Temple was destroyed when this city was sacked by Sennacherib.
Much of what is known about one king of this city comes from letters the king wrote to Sin-iddinam found in Larsa.
Prominent structures in this city included the E∙sag∙il∙a temple.
Necho II began a campaign against this city in the Battle of Carchemis, while this city also saw the reign of the Amorite and Kassite dynasties.
The Louvre Stele from this city records a series of “if/then” statements such as “if a man commits a robbery and is caught, that man will be killed.”
A ruler of the “neo” phase of this place destroyed the First Temple, while another formulated an “eye for an eye” based law code.
A “captivity” named for this city began after its forces sacked Judah.
Name this city home to Nebuchadnezzar and Hammurabi, as well as some namesake “hanging gardens.”
